newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's parliament urges Arabs to back Sudan.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's parliament urges Arabs to back Sudan.

text.p: Jordan's parliament urged Arab states on Monday to defend Sudan's military government against what it said was foreign aggression.

It said in a statement, carried by the official Petra news agency, that Sudan faced a grave threat from fighting which Sudanese rebels say has reached within 70 km (45 miles) of a major hydroelectric station on the Blue Nile.

"The Jordanian parliament...condemns and rejects this aggression which foreign parties are supporting and involved in, and considers it a glaring threat to Sudan's unity, security and stability," it said.

"(It) calls on the Arab nation to stand with Sudan in its battle and that the Arab League activate the joint Arab defence pact and raise the subject in international forums in support of Sudan," it added.
Jordan has given vocal support to the Sudanese government in the recent conflict.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, who on Saturday said Sudan was facing a conspiracy aimed at dividing up its territory, met visiting Sudanese Justice Minister Abdel Basit Sabdrat in Amman on Monday.

"Kabariti was the first Arab leader to raise his voice in support of Sudan," Sabdrat was quoted by Petra as saying after the meeting. Sabdrat repeated Sudanese government charges that Ethiopia and Eritrean forces were behind the fighting.
"There is an Eritrean plan to set up a state including parts of Sudan, Djibouti and the three islands (disputed with Yemen)," he said. "And Ethiopia is a thorn in the Arab community of the Red Sea."
Sudanese rebels, some of whom have waged a 13-year civil war against successive governments in Khartoum, say they alone are fighting the Islamist government.
The Jordanian parliament called on the rebels to patch up their row with Khartoum.
It said Jordan and other Arab countries should offer aid to Sudan and support it at the United Nations.

Sudan's northern neighbour Egypt, which hosts Sudanese opposition groups and says Sudan harbours and trains Moslem militants, has refused to help the Sudanese government. It says the fighting is an internal problem.
Jordan's Moslem Brotherhood said on Saturday the fighting in Sudan was part of a U.S.-Israeli conspiracy to separate southern Sudan from the north and plant a Zionist state in Africa.
